abstract: Senataxin (SETX) is an RNA/DNA helicase involved in transcription, RNA processing, R-loop resolution, and genome maintenance. Mutations in SETX cause neurological disorders, but its role in human motor neuron (MN) development remains unclear. Here, we examined SETX function using isogenic SETX knockout (KO) human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), shRNA-mediated knockdown, and direct conversion of fibroblasts into MNs. SETX expression increased during differentiation from hiPSCs to neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and MNs. SETX loss slowed hiPSC and NPC proliferation without preventing MN generation. However, SETX-deficient MNs developed shorter neurites, dystrophic swellings, and progressive neuronal loss. MEA recordings showed reduced firing and burst activity and almost no synchronized network bursts. RNA hybrid accumulation increased after SETX loss, with the largest relative increase in MNs among the cell types examined. RNA-seq revealed altered neurodevelopmental gene expression at the NPC stage and during MN differentiation, together with increased expression of stress- and apoptosis-associated genes. Proteomic analysis identified changes in proteins involved in neuronal structure, synaptic function, RNA regulation, and cellular homeostasis. Concordant decreases in selected RNAs and proteins supported disruption of neuronal structural and synaptic programs. Together, these findings reveal a stage-dependent requirement for SETX and identify SETX as an important regulator of transcriptional programs governing human MN maturation, function, and survival, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding the selective MN vulnerability associated with SETX-linked neurological diseases.
